claims.text: Successful homogeneous noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticle formation is governed by synchronization of constituent precursor reduction kinetics.
Nearly simultaneous precursor reduction produces nearly simultaneous nucleation.
A rapid thermal pulse can synchronize reduction of the constituent precursors.
Synchronized reduction or restricted mobility forces stochastic incorporation of all elements into a single-phase nanoparticle.
Stochastic incorporation under synchronized or mobility-limited conditions suppresses phase separation and elemental segregation.
A uniformly mixed solution or solid single-source precursor provides intimate contact among the constituent metal precursors.
The proposed processing modification can enforce nearly simultaneous reduction and nucleation of all constituent precursors.
Synchronized processing increases the density and uniformity of initial nucleation sites.
Restricted atomic diffusion kinetically traps atoms in a random, well-mixed configuration.
Concurrent nucleation leads to stochastic incorporation of all metal species.
Kinetic trapping can oppose elemental preferences arising from binary mixing enthalpies.
Asynchronous reduction causes some elements to nucleate earlier than others.
Early nucleation of selected elements promotes phase segregation and elemental inhomogeneity.
Synchronized reduction will yield more homogeneous, uniformly distributed, single-phase nanoparticles than a conventional asynchronous baseline.
Conventional broad-window reduction produces phase separation, elemental segregation, or secondary phases.
The mechanism applies primarily to noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles made by thermal or chemical reduction with controllable reduction kinetics and atomic mobility.
The mechanism may fail in high-temperature, solution-based, or ligand-dominated syntheses where atomic diffusion is high.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in homogeneity and single-phase character under synchronized conditions would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The initial state explicitly permits a solution precursor and the stated scope includes chemical reduction, while the boundary says the hypothesis may not be valid for solution-based synthesis. The subset of solution processing intended to remain in scope is not defined.

Rapid thermal treatment is proposed as a route to successful synchronization, but high-temperature synthesis is listed as a regime where the hypothesis may not apply; the temperature–time conditions distinguishing these regimes are unspecified.
